title: Value of One
context: Grade 4, the chapter's recap, and the one place where a division and a multiplication are used together on purpose. An adult sees a shopping sum. What is actually being taught is where to stop: at the value of one, which is found by dividing, then at the number the question wants, which is found by multiplying, and then at the unit the question counts in. One exercise gives rice for a number of people, and the rice one person needs is a part of a kilogram, which this chapter cannot write. The number of people one kilogram feeds is whole, and the chapter's own self-assessment says the value of one is found and vice versa, so the tool finds it either way round.

writeup.why: Find the value of one thing by dividing, the value of many by multiplying, and answer in exactly the units the question asks for.
writeup.look: Two rails across the stage, things on top and their value underneath, tied at every stop, with an answer slot and its unit at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Value of One' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the stops walked against the stops this question needs, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as the rails reach one and then the number wanted, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The things rail runs across the working area, 1000 by 110 at 100,256, counting things in amber at each stop, with the things themselves drawn there in rows of ten, a notebook, a ticket, a bag of rice. The value rail runs under it, 1000 by 110 at 100,420, carrying the value in deep blue, rupees or kilograms or people, and at every stop a near-black tie runs straight down between the two, so a number of things is never read without its value. The first stop holds what the story gives. Three keys stand along the foot, each 160 by 60 from 100,656: divide to one, which walks both rails back to one thing in a single movement and writes the value of one in green at that stop; multiply to many, which walks them out to the number the question wants, drawing each stop as it is passed; and turn, which swaps the two rails over so the value of one is found the other way round from the same first stop. The whole number lamp hangs over the right hand end of the rails at 1060,206 and lights whenever the way being walked comes out whole. A way that gives less than one of the unit is drawn stopping short of the tick for one, as a part, labelled as a part this chapter cannot write yet, never left blank and never rounded. When the rails are turned, the way just walked stays drawn as a record strip under them, 1000 by 44 at 100,546, with its own lamp lit or dark, so both ways stand on the stage together. The more bracket, 1000 by 44 at 100,600, spans only the stops between what the story already has and what the question adds, and measures that stretch alone. The converter stands at the lower right, 460 by 70 at 640,656, beside the answer column, and turns days into weeks in rows of seven and months into a year in rows of twelve. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a value or a count is asked for, with a unit strip under it, rupees, kilograms, people, days, weeks, months and a year, and the answer slot will not close on a number whose unit is not the one the question asks for. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The two rails never move apart. Whatever one rail does, the other does at the same stop in the same movement, because a value of one read off without its one thing is how the unit gets lost.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last story the child worked, both rails walked to one and out to many, and the answer standing in the unit the question asked for.

phases.win: both rails stop at one and the value of one settles on the lower rail
phases.does: walks both rails back to one thing and writes its value
phases.goal: the value of one is the value of many divided by how many there are
phases.says: How many things, and what do they cost? What does one cost?
phases.check: Away from the screen: seven bus tickets cost two hundred and ten rupees. What does one cost, and did you divide or multiply?
phases.feels: the value of many is shared out equally among the things, and one thing carries one share
phases.hands: Put four identical pencils in a bag with a price tag of forty-eight rupees. Ask what one pencil costs, and let the class say how they would find out before anyone works it out. Then take one pencil out and write its price on a tag of its own.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many things are at the first stop? Second rung, the phase's: what is the value of all of them? Third rung: the rails are cut to two things costing twenty rupees, and the child walks them back to one. The number pad and the unit strip stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a price and a count are in the question together, and multiplying is the move a shopping sum usually wants.
wrong.move: multiplies two hundred and seventy by six instead of dividing, which gives the cost of thirty-six notebooks.
wrong.screen: the rails are walked the child's way, out from six notebooks to thirty-six, and the value rail reads one thousand six hundred and twenty rupees there, the child's number at a stop with thirty-six things above it. The rails are then walked back from six to one, and forty-five rupees settles under one notebook. Both stops stay drawn along the rails.

wrong.why: a division needs one number on each side, and the smaller number written first looks like the thing being shared.
wrong.move: divides six by two hundred and seventy, which asks how many notebooks one rupee buys, and gets stuck.
wrong.screen: the turn control shows the child's way round, with the notebooks on the lower rail, and walking back to one rupee stops short of the tick for one notebook, a part drawn and labelled as a part. The lamp lights over the other way, where one notebook is forty-five rupees, and both ways stay drawn.

phases.screen: the two rails at the first stop, holding a number of things and their value
phases.soWhat: The value of one is the value of many divided by how many there are.
phases.concept: Find the value of one first

phases.win: the rails stop at the number wanted and its value lands in the answer slot
phases.does: walks the rails out from one to the number wanted by multiplying
phases.goal: the value of many is the value of one times how many are needed
phases.says: You know what one costs. How much for the number you need?
phases.check: One mango costs twenty-three rupees. What do eleven mangoes cost? Say whether you needed to divide at all.
phases.feels: once one thing is priced, any number of them is only that price again and again
phases.hands: With one pencil's price written on its own tag, ask what five pencils cost, then twelve, then thirty, and write each on the board beside the one before. Ask what the class did every time, and whether they ever needed to go back to the bag of four.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is one worth? Second rung, the phase's: how many does the question want? Third rung: the rails are cut to one thing worth five rupees and walked out to three, a stop at a time. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the unitary method was just met as a division, and the second step is heard as more of the same.
wrong.move: divides again at the second step, because the first step was a division.
wrong.screen: the child's division is walked on the rails and lands at a stop where fourteen notebooks would cost less than one notebook did, which the rails draw and leave standing. Multiply to many then walks out from one to fourteen, the value rail climbing by forty-five rupees at every stop, and six hundred and thirty rupees settles under fourteen notebooks.

wrong.why: the price in the story is the number printed on the page, and the value of one had to be made rather than read.
wrong.move: multiplies the price of all nine tickets by four, as if four were a number of lots of nine.
wrong.screen: the rails stop at thirty-six tickets for the child's four thousand three hundred and twenty rupees, and that stop stays drawn. The rails are then walked back from nine to one ticket, one hundred and twenty rupees, and out again to four, four hundred and eighty, with both walks left standing.

phases.screen: the rails standing at one thing, with the number the question wants lit further along
phases.soWhat: The value of many is the value of one times how many are needed.

phases.win: the converter turns the days into weeks and the answer settles in the unit asked
phases.does: reads the unit in the answer slot and changes the result into it
phases.goal: the answer is given in the units the question asks for, and how much more is the extra part only
phases.says: What does the question count in? Is your number in that?
phases.check: Save twenty rupees a day for a game that costs one thousand four hundred rupees. Say the days first, then the weeks.
phases.feels: the working can be finished and the question still not answered, until the number is in the units the question counts
phases.hands: A child saves ten rupees a day for a ball that costs one hundred and forty rupees. Work it with the class and stop when the division gives a number of days. Ask the class to read the question's last words again and say whether the number on the board answers them. Then ask the question again for weeks.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what unit is your number in? Second rung, the phase's: what does the question count in? Third rung: the converter is cut to fourteen days, and the child lays them out in rows of seven. The number pad and the unit strip stay open.

wrong.why: the division was the hard part and its answer is the last number standing, so it feels like the end.
wrong.move: answers fifty-six because it came out of the division, when the question asked for weeks.
wrong.screen: the answer slot shows weeks written after its box and hands the fifty-six back, still written beside it, with the unit strip lighting days against the child's number. The converter then lays the days out in rows of seven, eight rows, and eight weeks settles in the slot.

wrong.why: the whole stay is what the story is about, and the word more reads like a word for a bigger total.
wrong.move: answers five thousand four hundred rupees, the cost of all nine days, when the question asked how much more two extra days cost.
wrong.screen: the more bracket opens over only the two stops beyond the week the story already paid for, and measures one thousand two hundred rupees there. The child's total stays written beside the rails, the week's four thousand two hundred is lit as already paid, and the two numbers are shown to differ by exactly that week.

phases.screen: a finished working whose result is in days, with the answer slot asking for weeks
phases.soWhat: The answer is given in the units the question asks for, and how much more is the extra part only.
phases.concept: Answer the question that was asked

phases.win: the lamp lights over the whole number way and the answer comes out whole
phases.does: tries the first way, sees a part, turns the rails, and finds the whole number value
phases.goal: the value of one can be found either way round, and the way that comes out whole is the one to use
phases.says: This way gives less than one. Can you turn it round?
phases.check: Twelve kilograms of flour make bread for three hundred people. How much flour do five hundred people need? Say which value of one you found.
phases.feels: the value of one does not have to be the value of one person, it can be what one kilogram does
phases.hands: Put a two kilogram bag of rice beside a card saying it feeds forty people. Ask how much rice one person needs, and let the class find that they cannot write it yet. Then ask how many people one kilogram feeds, and work out how many kilograms sixty people need.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: does this way give less than one? Second rung, the phase's: what happens if the rails are turned round? Third rung: the rails are cut to two kilograms feeding twenty people, and the child turns them and finds what one kilogram feeds. The number pad and the unit strip stay open.

wrong.why: the method was taught as finding the value of one person first, and that value is a part this chapter has no way to write.
wrong.move: insists on the rice for one person, finds it is a part of a kilogram, and says the question cannot be done.
wrong.screen: the rails walk back to one person and stop short of the tick for one kilogram, the part drawn and labelled as a part not yet writable, and left standing. The turn control then swaps the rails, walks the kilograms back to one, and fifteen people settles under one kilogram with the lamp lit over it. Seven hundred and twenty people are then walked out to forty-eight kilograms.

wrong.why: the method was learnt as divide then multiply, and turning the rails round does not change the order the hands remember.
wrong.move: turns the rails round and then multiplies seven hundred and twenty by fifteen, because the second step of the method was a multiplication.
wrong.screen: the child's ten thousand eight hundred kilograms is drawn at its stop on the kilogram rail, far past the thirty that fed four hundred and fifty people, with the people rail above it reading only seven hundred and twenty. The rails are then walked from one kilogram feeding fifteen people out to seven hundred and twenty people, fifteen at a stop, and forty-eight kilograms settles there.

phases.screen: a story where one way round gives less than one of the unit, with the turn control waiting
phases.soWhat: The value of one can be found either way round, and the way that comes out whole is the one to use.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when the turn control is pressed on a way that gave a part. The two rails lift and cross over each other in one smooth movement, the ties staying taut between them the whole time, so the kilograms land on top and the people underneath. Divide to one then walks the turned rails back to one kilogram, the lamp lights over them, and a whole number of people settles at that stop, while the part from the first way stays drawn short of one on the record strip below. Turn it back and forth as often as a finger likes; the lamp follows the whole number way each time, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the two rails stand at their first stop, holding a number of things and their value, with the divide control lit and nothing walked. On the second the rails already stand at one thing with the value of one written under it, and the number the question wants is lit further along. On the third a finished working stands on the rails with its result in days, and the answer slot asks for weeks with the converter closed beside it. On the fourth the rails stand at a first stop where walking back to one person lands short of one kilogram, and the turn control waits. The running count at the top left holds the stops walked against the stops this question needs, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first stop, or the lit number wanted, or the unit in the answer slot, or the turn control, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what one of them is worth. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.

writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on finding the value of one, multiplying up to many, answering in the units asked, and choosing which way round to find the value of one.

source_tool.description: Two rails run across the stage, one above the other, the top rail counting things and the bottom rail carrying their value, joined by a tie at each stop so a number of things is always read with its value. The first stop holds what the story gives, such as a number of scarves and what they cost. A divide control walks both rails back to one thing and writes the value of one, and a multiply control walks them out again to the number the question wants. A turn control swaps the rails, so the value of one can be found either way round: the cost of one thing or the things one rupee buys, the rice one person needs or the people one kilogram feeds. A whole number lamp lights over whichever way comes out whole, and a way that would give a part of a unit is drawn as a part, less than one, and labelled as not yet writable in this chapter rather than left blank. An answer slot at the right carries the unit the question asks for, with a converter beside it from days to weeks and from months to a year, and a more bracket measures only the extra part when a question asks how much more.
source_tool.art_direction: Two rails, things above and value below / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a tray of counters and a row of plates, digit cards under place headings, sticks tied in bundles, a long division frame with its bracket, a ladder of multiples, a strip of cells, a story card, and two rails tied at every stop.

Equal shares are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a plate or a part is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are on it, and anything counted one at a time is drawn in rows of ten so that no more than twenty loose things ever have to be counted singly.

What is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the shares, in a dish or a slot of its own, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never tucked under a share and never left to be guessed from a gap.
A division is always written with every place headed. The number being divided at a step is shown with its place name, so fifteen tens is never drawn as a bare fifteen.

Every zero in a quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as the other digits and is never dimmed, shrunk or dropped. A zero is written only where the number being divided is smaller than the divisor, and a leading zero may stand or be left off, but a zero after the first digit always stands.
What is left at every step is drawn in its own slot before the next digit comes down, and it slides down to join that digit so the next number can be seen being made.
A remainder is written as a number. A zero standing in front of its other digits is lifted off and set aside, never written into the answer.
No stage ever shows a number for a division by zero. Where one is asked, the stage says it is not possible and draws nothing to share into.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a counter, a digit or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; and what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion. Those four hold from the plates to the frame to the story card in every tool of this chapter. A multiple of the divisor, whether it is being tried on the ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose, so the chunks can be added up without being mistaken for the share. A zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey, and grey never means faint: it is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, because it is holding a place. All of that holds in greyscale, because what is left over is told apart by the dish or the left slot it sits in, and a quotient digit by the row it sits in, before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

phase_map.concept: Find the value of one first
Answer the question that was asked

placement.where: At the end of the chapter, once packs from a price list have been priced one item at a time by hand. The tool is what holds both ways of finding the value of one on the stage at once and lights the one that comes out whole, which a single written line cannot show.

answer_key.rule: The unitary method finds the value of one unit first and then the value of the number needed. The value of one is found by dividing the value of many by how many there are, and the value of many by multiplying the value of one by how many are needed. The value of one can be found either way round: the value of one thing, or how many things one unit of value covers. Use the way that comes out whole. Give the answer in the units the question asks for, changing days to weeks or months to a year where the question counts in those. When a question asks how much more, the answer is the value of the extra part only, not the total.
answer_key.wrong: The rails are walked back to one and out again a stop at a time, the unit the question asks for is lit in the answer slot, and the turn control shows the other way round. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The cost of 6 notebooks is known, and the cost of one is wanted.
One notebook costs 270 rupees shared among 6, so divide 270 by 6.
27 tens divided by 6 is 4 tens with 3 tens left, and 30 ones divided by 6 is 5, so one notebook costs 45 rupees.
items.question: 6 notebooks cost 270 rupees. What does one notebook cost?
items.checkpoint: The value of one unit is found by dividing the value of many by how many there are.
items.misconception: Multiplying 270 by 6 instead of dividing, which gives 1620 rupees, the cost of 36 notebooks.

steps: The value of one notebook, 45 rupees, is already known.
Many notebooks cost the value of one times how many: 45 times 14.
45 times 10 is 450 and 45 times 4 is 180, so 14 notebooks cost 630 rupees.
items.question: One notebook costs 45 rupees. What do 14 notebooks cost?
items.checkpoint: Once the value of one is known, multiply it by the number needed.
items.misconception: Dividing again at the second step, because the first step was a division.

steps: Each day adds 35 rupees, so the number of days is 1960 divided by 35, which is 56.
56 is a number of days, but the question counts in weeks.
A week is 7 days, so 56 divided by 7 is 8, and the answer is 8 weeks.
items.answer: 8 weeks, because 1960 divided by 35 is 56 days, and 56 days is 8 weeks
items.question: A child saves 35 rupees every day for a bat that costs 1960 rupees. How many weeks will the saving take?
items.checkpoint: Give the answer in the units the question asks for, and change units when they do not match.
items.misconception: Answering 56 because it came out of the division, when the question asked for weeks.

steps: The rice for one person is 30 divided by 450, which is less than one kilogram, a part this chapter cannot write.
So find the value of one the other way round: one kilogram feeds 450 divided by 30, which is 15 people.
720 people need 720 divided by 15 kilograms, which is 48 kg. Check: 48 kilograms feed 48 times 15, which is 720 people.
items.answer: 48 kg, found through the number of people one kilogram feeds
items.question: 30 kg of rice feeds 450 people. How much rice will 720 people need?
items.checkpoint: The value of one can be found either way round, and the way that comes out whole is the one to use.
items.misconception: Stopping because 30 kilograms cannot be shared among 450 people in whole kilograms, instead of turning the question round.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: 5 bags of flour weigh 135 kg. What does one bag weigh?
A pen costs 18 rupees. What do 12 pens cost?
9 tickets cost 1080 rupees. What do 4 tickets cost?
items.final_answer: 480 rupees, because one ticket costs 120 rupees and 4 times 120 is 480

items.question: A room costs 4200 rupees for a week. How much more will the stay cost if it runs for 2 more days?
items.final_answer: 1200 rupees more. One day costs 600 rupees, and the question asks for the 2 extra days only, not the 5400 rupees of the whole 9 days

items.question: A child saves 45 rupees a day. How many weeks will it take to save 2835 rupees?
items.final_answer: 9 weeks, because 2835 divided by 45 is 63 days, and 63 days is 9 weeks

items.question: 16 kg of rice feeds 400 people. How much rice do 650 people need? Say which value of one you found.
items.final_answer: 26 kg. The rice for one person is less than a kilogram, so find the people one kilogram feeds instead: 400 divided by 16 is 25, and 650 divided by 25 is 26

items.question: 4 buses carry 180 children, the same number in each. How many buses are needed for 315 children? Which value of one comes out whole here?
items.final_answer: 7 buses. The children for one bus, 45, comes out whole; one child's share of a bus does not. 315 divided by 45 is 7

items.question: The school fee for 4 months is 10,000 rupees. What is the fee for a whole year?
items.final_answer: 30,000 rupees. One month costs 2500 rupees, and a year is 12 months, so 2500 times 12 is 30,000

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: counts the things at each stop
carries the value of the things at each stop, tied to the rail above
walks both rails back to one thing and writes its value
walks both rails out to the number the question wants
swaps the rails, so the value of one is found the other way round
lights over the way round that comes out whole
changes days to weeks and months to a year beside the answer slot
measures only the extra part when the question asks how much more

teaching_notes: Price a pack from a list before the tool is opened: what one item costs, then what a different number costs. Then use the tool for the two things a written line cannot show. It holds both ways of finding the value of one at once, and it keeps the unit the question asks for in front of the child until the answer is in it. The worked example for this topic buys eight scarves for twelve hundred rupees and finds that ten cost one thousand five hundred rupees, and it is numbered ten; there is no example nine anywhere in the chapter, so nobody needs to look for it. Three of the exercise questions divide cleanly the taught way. The rice question does not: the rice one person needs is a part of a kilogram, which this chapter has no way to write. One kilogram feeds a whole number of people, so find that instead. The chapter's own self-assessment says the value of one is found and vice versa, and either way round is exactly that. Watch the hostel question, which asks how much more a longer stay costs, so its answer is the cost of the extra days and not of the whole stay, and the saving question, which asks for weeks, so the days the division gives are not the answer. The self-assessment has six lines. One of them says the child can estimate a quotient, which the chapter never teaches, so a child cannot honestly tick it from this chapter; say so rather than letting it pass.
generation_prompt: Build a unitary method tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Two rails run across the working area one above the other, the top rail counting things and the bottom rail carrying their value, with a tie drawn between them at every stop so a number of things is always read with its value. The first stop holds what the story gives. A divide control walks both rails back to one thing and writes the value of one, and a multiply control walks them out to the number the question wants, drawing each stop as it is reached. A turn control swaps the two rails so the value of one can be found either way round. A whole number lamp lights over whichever way comes out whole; a way that gives less than one of the unit is drawn as a part of a unit, short of the tick for one, and labelled as a part this chapter cannot write yet, never left blank or rounded. An answer slot fixed down the right of the canvas carries the unit the question asks for, with a converter beside it from days to weeks and from months to a year, and a more bracket that measures only the extra part when the question asks how much more. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Find what one costs by dividing. Find what many cost by multiplying. If one way gives less than one, turn it round. Answer in the units the question asks for.
